title.en: The Ugly Boy Who Could Not Be Moved

region.zh: 漢京貴族宅（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Collected by Im Bang; English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'The Awful Little Goblin', eBook #51002

summary.en: At a great feast in a nobleman's house an uncombed, ugly boy of fifteen appears in the women's quarters and will not go. Servants, then ten men with ropes, then giants with clubs try to move or crush him — he is like a rock fast in the earth, and the club-blows sound like reverberating thunder without turning a hair of him. The crowd, fearing this is not a man but a god, bow and supplicate until he gives a sarcastic smile, goes out of the gate and disappears. From that day the people of the house are taken ill; those who scolded him, tied him and pounded him all die within a few days. It was commonly held that the boy was the Too-uk Spirit.
summary.zh: 漢京貴族宴客，有垢面醜童忽然立於婦人房前，喝之不去。以繩縛、以巨木擊，皆如撼山擊卵，童子紋絲不動。眾懼，以為神，羅拜乞哀。童冷笑而出，旋杳。自是闔家及諸客相繼病歿。俗謂此即土尤之神云。

passages.text: There was an occasion for a celebration in the home of a nobleman of Seoul. In front of the women's quarters there suddenly appeared an uncombed, ugly-looking boy about fifteen years of age. One of the women guests sent a servant to reprimand him and put him out, but the boy stood stock-still with no word of reply.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Awful Little Goblin' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: Several took hold of him to pull him, but he was like a fixed rock fast in the earth, absolutely immovable. They sent ten strong men with ropes to bind him, but like a giant mountain he remained fast; five or six giant fellows with clubs laid on with all their might, the sound of their pounding like reverberating thunder, yet not a hair did he turn, not a wink did he give. The crowd began to fear, saying, 'This is not a man, but a god,' so they entered the courtyard, one and all, and began to bow before him, joining their hands and supplicating earnestly.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Awful Little Goblin' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: At last the boy gave a sarcastic smile, turned round, went out of the gate and disappeared. The company, frightened out of their wits, called off the feast. From that day on, the people of that house were taken ill, including host and guests; those who scolded him, those who tied him with ropes, those who pounded him, all died in a few days. It was commonly held that the boy was the Too-uk Spirit.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Awful Little Goblin' (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: God's Way: The Lightning Strikes the Mother-Beater

region.en: Buckwheat field outside a country town (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 郊野蕎麥田（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Tale by Yi Ryuk; English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'God's Way', eBook #51002

summary.en: A man of fierce and ungovernable disposition beats his mother, who screams: 'Oh, God, why do you not strike dead this wicked man who beats his mother?' Thrusting his sickle through his belt he goes to reap buckwheat under a fine clear sky — until a dark fleck of cloud appears in mid-heaven and all the sky becomes black. Furious thunder follows; the villagers see in the field a man with lifted sickle trying to ward off the flashes, and when the storm clears they find the mother-beater struck dead and riven to pieces. God takes note of evil doers on this earth, and deals with them as they deserve.
summary.zh: 有悍夫常毆其母，母呼天曰：『天何不殛此逆子！』其人攜鐮往田刈蕎。晴空萬里，忽黑雲一點，頃刻天晦，雷雨大作。村人遙見田中一人舉鐮遮雷。雨霧往視，則逆子已遭雷殛，碎裂於地。天道報應，可不畏哉。

sensitivity.note: Moral exemplum of filial piety; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: In a certain town there lived a man of fierce and ungovernable disposition, who in moments of anger used to beat his mother. One day, thus beaten, the parent screamed out, 'Oh, God, why do you not strike dead this wicked man who beats his mother?'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'God's Way' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: The son thrust his sickle through his belt and went slowly off to the fields where he was engaged by a neighbour in reaping buckwheat. The day was fine and the sky beautifully clear, when suddenly a dark fleck of cloud appeared in mid-heaven, and a little later all the sky became black. Furious thunder followed, and rain came on.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'God's Way' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: The village people looked out toward the field, where the flashes of lightning were specially noticeable; they seemed to see there a man with lifted sickle trying to ward them off. When the storm had cleared away, they went to see, and lo, they found the man who had beaten his mother struck dead and riven to pieces.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'God's Way' (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: The Old Man in the Dream Beseeches for the Turtle

texts.period: Tale by Yi Ryuk; English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'The Old Man in the Dream', eBook #51002

summary.en: Kwon Jai, high in rank and given to sport, dreams that an old man bows low in tears: 'Sir, Minister Hong wishes to kill off me and all my posterity. Please save me — if you desist, Hong will give it up and I shall live and all mine.' A rap at the door wakes him: it is Hong, come to invite him to fish for turtles at Lotus Lake. Then Kwon knows the turtle appeared in the dream in the form of an old man, and declines, saying he is ill — and he learned later that Hong also did not go.
summary.zh: 權居士夢一老人泣拜曰：『洪公欲盡誅吾族，公救之。』覺而洪公適來邀，往蓮池釣龜。權悟夢中之老人即龜也，辭以疾。後聞洪公亦未往。

sensitivity.note: Animal-dream omen tale; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: Kwon Jai was a man high in rank and well advanced in years, much given to sport and various kinds of pleasure. One night he had a dream, when an old man came to him, bowed low, and in tears said, 'Sir, Minister Hong wishes to kill off me and all my posterity. Please save me, won't you?'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Old Man in the Dream' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'Hong will assuredly ask Your Excellency to help him. Desist from it, please, for if you do, Hong will give it up and I shall live and all mine,' said the old man. A little later there came a rap at the door, when Kwon awakened and asked, 'Who is there?' It was Hong, who that day had planned an excursion to Lotus Lake to fish for turtles, and now had come specially to invite Kwon to go with him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Old Man in the Dream' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then Kwon knew that the turtle had appeared to him in a dream in the form of an old man, so he declined, saying he was ill. It was learned later that Hong also did not go.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Old Man in the Dream' (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: Softy, the Priest Who Took the Floggings

texts.period: Tale by Yi Ryuk; English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'The Perfect Priest', eBook #51002

summary.en: A priest called Namnu has perfected his ways in Buddhist doctrine: he undresses and gives his clothing to the cold, and everybody calls him Softy. Whenever he sees anyone sentenced to a flogging in the temple or official yamen, he invariably begs to take the culprit's place. At a great function at Pagoda Temple he tells Prince Hong of Yon-san, 'You are indeed a very great man,' takes a box on the ear, and laughs: 'Please, Hong, don't do that, it hurts! it hurts!' Before the Temple he looks at Prince Yi and says, 'I know your face, but I have forgotten your name. Oh, I remember now, you are Yi Sok-hyong' — to the scandal of the monastery priests, who hurry to apologize: 'Softy was born so, God made him so.'
summary.zh: 有僧曰南婁，戒行圓滿，遇寒者輒解衣衣之，人呼曰軟和尚。凡見受笞者必以身代。於塔寺大會中謂燕山君之子曰『公真偉人也』，被批頰，笑曰『勿爾，痛哉』。又於寺前直呼親王名諱，僧眾大驚謝罪，曰『此天生如此，惟乞恕之』。

sensitivity.note: Holy-fool (holy fool/palmun) figure in Buddhist context; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: There was once a priest called Namnu who had perfected his ways in the Buddhistic doctrine. Whenever he had clothing of his own he would willingly undress and give it to those who were cold. His spirit was gentle, with no creases or corners in it. Everybody, high and low, rich and poor, called him by the nickname of Softy.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Perfect Priest' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: Whenever he saw any one sentenced to a flogging in the temple or official yamen, Namnu invariably begged that he might take the culprit's place. Once, when there was a great function in progress at Pagoda Temple and many high officials were assembled, Softy, too, was seen kneeling at the side. He suddenly remarked to Prince Hong of Yon-san, 'You are indeed a very great man.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Perfect Priest' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: Hong replied, 'What do you mean by great man, you impudent brat? Take that,' and gave him a box with his fist on the ear. Softy laughed, and said, 'Please, Hong, don't do that, it hurts! it hurts!' Later, stopping before the Temple with Prince Yi and other high officials, Softy looked at Yi and said, 'I know your face, but I have forgotten your name. Afterwards he said, Oh, I remember now, you are Yi Sok-hyong.' The priests of the monastery who heard this familiarity were scandalized, and hurried to make no end of apology to the Prince: 'Softy was born so, God made him so. Please, Your Excellency, forgive him.' The Prince forgave him and so he was not disturbed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Perfect Priest' (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: The Propitious Magpie and the Imitation Nest

region.en: Outside the South Gate, Seoul (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 漢城南門外（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Tale by Yi Ryuk (1439-1498), with personal testimony; English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'The Propitious Magpie', eBook #51002

summary.en: People say that when the magpie builds its nest directly south of a home, the master of the house will be promoted. King T'ai-jong's poor friend, failing in all his projects, sends a servant to build an imitation magpie's nest in a propitious place before the royal procession; caught and questioned, the servant explains the belief, and the King takes pity and orders the appointment at once. Yi Ryuk testifies from his own life: as a boy he moved a fallen nest to a propitious tree south of his home, and that very winter his father was promoted three degrees; when a slave pulled down the nest at his Chong-pa summer-house the magpies built again the next year, and in that year Ye-jong came to the throne and Yi was promoted again; a third nest by his office brought a third promotion. 'There is a spiritual power in the magpie surely.'
summary.zh: 俗云鵲巢於宅南者，主人必遷官。太宗有貧友，遣僕於蹕路造偽鵲巢以邀福；事發，僕直陳其故，王憐而即予除目。柳夢寅自記：少時移鵲巢於宅南楮樹，其冬父連升三級；後館前鵲巢被婢拆作薪，次年復營，是年睿宗即位而柳復遷官。鵲之有靈，信矣。

passages.text: People say that when the magpie builds its nest directly south of a home, the master of the house will be promoted in office. King T'ai-jong had a friend once who was very poor and had failed in all his projects; he decided to wait till the King went out on procession and then send a servant to build an imitation magpie's nest in some propitious place before him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Propitious Magpie' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: The King saw it and asked the man what he was doing. He said in reply that when a magpie builds its nest straight south of a home the master of the house instantly gets promotion; his master had waited so long and nothing had come, that he was building an imitation nest to bring it about. The King took pity on him and ordered his appointment at once.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Propitious Magpie' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: When I was young myself a magpie built its nest before our home, but with other boys I cut off the branch so that the whole nest fell to the ground; feeling sorry and afraid, on a propitious site to the south I had the nest hung up on a tree, where the young all lived and flourished and flew away. In that very winter my father was promoted three degrees in rank. Afterwards, before my summer-house at Chong-pa, magpies built a nest in a date tree; a woman slave pulled it down for fuel, but they came again the next year and built once more, and that year Ye-jong came to the throne and I was promoted again. In the spring of 1471 magpies built their nest in a tree just south of my office: 'There is a spiritual power in the magpie surely, as men have said from olden times and as I myself have proven.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Propitious Magpie' (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: The Old Buddha Rides Past the Magistrates

region.zh: 鶏龍縣江干（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Tale by Yi Ryuk; English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'The Old Buddha', eBook #51002

summary.en: Prime Minister Choi Yun-tok, mourning his mother, rides south with a single horse and one servant through the county of Kai-ryong, where district magistrates are drinking under a tent by the riverbank. Offended that the mourner does not dismount, they arrest his servant and demand his master's name. 'Choi, the Old Buddha.' 'But what's his real name?' 'The old Buddha.' Beaten over the head, the servant says slowly: he is called Choi the Buddha, but his real name is Yun-tok, on his way to his country home in Chang-won. The magistrates recognize the Prime Minister, strike their tent, clear away the eatables, and run to make their deepest salaam and ask pardon for their sin.
summary.zh: 崔有敦相公居喪南行，道經鶏龍縣。縣令宴於江亭，怒其不下馬，逮其僕問主人名。僕曰『老佛崔公』；再問，曰『老佛』。笞之，僕徐言曰『佛者字也，諱有敦，今往昌原私第』。令等大懼，撤席奔拜請罪。老佛者，相公之別號也。

passages.text: Prime Minister Choi Yun-tok was in mourning once for his mother. With a single horse and one servant he made a journey to the south where the road led through the county of Kai-ryong. At that very time two or three of the district magistrates had pitched a tent on the bank of the river and were having refreshments.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Old Buddha' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: They said to one another, 'Who is that mourner that goes riding by without dismounting? It must be some country farmer who has never learned proper manners. We shall certainly have to teach him a lesson.' They sent an attendant to arrest and bring his servant, and asked who his master was. 'Choi, the Old Buddha.' 'But what's his real name?' 'The old Buddha.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Old Buddha' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then they grew very angry and beat him over the head. Then the servant said slowly, 'He is called Choi the Buddha, but his real name is Yun-tok, and he is now on his way to his country home in Chang-won.' At once they recognized that it was no other than the Prime Minister, and great fear overcame them. They struck their tent, cleared away the eatables, and ran to make their deepest salaam and to ask pardon for their sin.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Old Buddha' (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: The Kill-Devil Pills of Prince Cheung

texts.period: Tale by Yi Ryuk; English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'A Wonderful Medicine', eBook #51002

summary.en: Prince Cheung, First Minister for thirty years and now nearly ninety, has his home attacked by goblins and devils: in broad daylight they snatch the hat from a young official's head and crumple it, and keep throwing stones till the whole court is in confusion. The Prince escapes to another house, prepares a special medicine called sal-kwi-whan, kill-devil-pills, which he offers in prayer — and from that time the goblins depart. After five or six years no sign of them has reappeared, and Prince Cheung is well and strong and free from sickness.
summary.zh: 張相公府中為鬼所擾，白晝擲石，奪客之帽而揉之，闔宅大亂。相公避居別第，製藥曰殺鬼丸，持咒服之。自是群鬼遁去，五六載不復至，相公亦康強無恙。

passages.text: Prince Cheung had been First Minister of the land for thirty years, a man just and upright, now nearly ninety years of age. His home was suddenly attacked by goblins and devils: when a young official came to call on him, these mysterious beings in broad daylight snatched the hat from his head and crumpled it up.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'A Wonderful Medicine' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: They threw stones, too, and kept on throwing them so that all the court was reduced to confusion. Prince Cheung made his escape and went to live in another house, where he prepared a special medicine called sal-kwi-whan, kill-devil-pills, which he offered in prayer. From that time the goblins departed, and now after five or six years no sign of them has reappeared; Prince Cheung, too, is well and strong and free from sickness.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'A Wonderful Medicine' (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: Mo, the Slave Wife Who Died Rather than Part

texts.period: Tale by Yi Ryuk, told by kin of the scholar An Yun; English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'Faithful Mo', eBook #51002

summary.en: An Yun, a noted scholar, loves Mo, the beautiful daughter of Prince Ha's slave, and takes her for his wife. The furious Prince has her arrested to marry her to one of his bondsmen; she escapes over the wall back to An, and together they swear to die rather than be parted. Arrested again, she is found hanging by the neck dead. Months later, returning from the Confucian Temple over Camel Mountain ridge in the autumn moonlight, An is musing love verses to her memory when a soft footfall comes from among the pines — there is Mo. Knowing her long dead, he runs to catch her hand: 'How did you come here?' — and she disappears. He cries out, falls ill, cannot swallow, and dies of a broken heart. 'Faithful unto death was she. Even of the faithful among the ancients was there ever a better than Mo?'
summary.zh: 安允與婢女無娘私結為夫婦，主人家怒而執之。無娘踰牆歸安，誓死不離。再被捕，縊死。後安自廟還，月夜過駱山嶺，忽聞松間履聲，則無娘也。安知其鬼，然情不能自已，趨執其手，瞬息而滅。安慟而病，粒食不下，遂卒。或曰：『至死靡他，雖士族之婦有不及者。』

sensitivity.note: Love-tragedy ghost tale; depicts Joseon slave status; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: Prince Ha had a slave who was a landed proprietor and lived in Yang-ju county; he had a daughter, fairest of the fair, whom he called Mo. An Yun was a noted scholar, a man of distinction in letters. He saw Mo, fell in love with her and took her for his wife. Prince Ha heard of this and was furiously angry: 'How is it that you, a slave, dare to marry with a man of the aristocracy?'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Faithful Mo' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: He had her arrested and brought home, intending to marry her to one of his bondsmen. Mo learned of this with tears and sorrow, made her escape over the wall and went back to An; together they took an oath to die rather than to be parted. Later Prince Ha sent his underlings to arrest her again and carry her off; after this all trace of her was lost till Mo was discovered one day in a room hanging by the neck dead.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Faithful Mo' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: Months of sorrow passed over An till once, under cover of the night, he was returning from the Confucian Temple to his house over the ridge of Camel Mountain. It was early autumn and the wooded tops were shimmering in the moonlight. Musing longingly of Mo, and repeating love verses to her memory, he suddenly heard a soft footfall as though coming from among the pines — there was Mo. An knew that she was long dead, but because he was so buried in thought of her, doubting nothing, he ran to her and caught her by the hand, saying, 'How did you come here?' — but she disappeared. An gave a great cry and broke into tears. He fell ill; a little later he died of a broken heart.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Faithful Mo' (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: The Minister in Plain Clothes and the Proud Scholar

region.zh: 南行道旁亭（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Tale by Yi Ryuk; English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'The Renowned Maing', eBook #51002

summary.en: Minister of State Maing Sa-song, dressed in plain clothes, is overtaken by rain and shelters in a side pavilion where the young scholar Whang Eui-hon, hands behind his back, reads the verse-boards. 'Well, grand-dad, do you know the flavour of verses like these?' The Minister pretends ignorance and asks the meaning; Whang lectures him on the great men of the past and living pictures in poetry. Then pack-horses, servants, tent poles and canvas packs come in a long procession, and Whang, to his amazement, learns the old man is Maing Sa-song, and drops unconsciously onto his knees in a deep and long obeisance. The Minister laughs: 'There is no difference in the value of mere men; they are high or low according to the thoughts that prompt them, but unfortunately all are born with a proud heart. You are not a common scholar; why, therefore, should you be so proud to begin with and so humble now?' — and comforts him and sends him away.
summary.zh: 蕭瑟松微服南行，避雨於亭。有書生黃義憲方負手讀壁上題詠，傲然問曰『老丈解此詩味否』。松佯為不知，請其講解。俄而行李駝馬續至，黃始知即蕭相公，不覺長跪。松笑曰：『人之貴賤在乎其心，而不在於貌。子始倨而後恭，何也？』乃慰而遣之。

passages.text: Minister of State Maing Sa-song once upon a time, dressed in plain clothes, started south on a long journey. On the way he was overtaken by rain, and turned into a side pavilion for rest and shelter. There was a young scholar already in the pavilion by the name of Whang Eui-hon, who with his two hands behind his back was reading the pavilion inscription board.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Renowned Maing' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: At last he turned to the old man and said, 'Well, grand-dad, do you know the flavour of verses like these?' The famous Minister, pretending ignorance, arose and said, 'An old countryman like myself, could you expect him to know? Please tell me the meaning.' Whang said, 'These verses were written by the great men of the past. What they saw and experienced they wrote down to inspire the souls of those who were to come after them. They are like pictures of sea and land, for there are living pictures in poetry, you know.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Renowned Maing' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: A little later came pack-horses loaded with all sorts of things, servants and retainers, tent poles, canvas packs and other equipment, a long procession. Whang, surprised, made inquiry, and to his amazement learned that the old man was none other than Maing Sa-song; unconsciously he dropped onto his knees in a deep and long obeisance. The Minister laughed and said, 'That will do; there is no difference in the value of mere men, they are high or low according to the thoughts that prompt them, but unfortunately all are born with a proud heart. You are not a common scholar; why, therefore, should you be so proud to begin with and so humble now?' The Minister took him by the hand, led him to his mat, made him sit down, comforted him and sent him away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Renowned Maing' (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: Who Decides, God or the King?

region.zh: 漢城慶熙宮（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Tale by Yi Ryuk; story of King Tae-jong (r. 1400-1418); English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'Who Decides, God or the King?', eBook #51002

summary.en: Resting in Heung-yang Palace, King Tae-jong overhears two eunuchs arguing whether riches and honour are in the king's hand or ordered of God. To test it, he writes a secret despatch — 'Raise the bearer of this letter one degree in rank' — and commands A to deliver it. At the palace gate a furious pain takes A in the stomach, and he begs B to go in his place. The next day the record of promotions shows B advanced, and not one word about A. King Tae-jong makes inquiry, and when he knows the circumstances he gives a sudden start of wonder and remains long in deep thought.
summary.zh: 太宗休於宮中，聞二閹辯富貴由王抑由天。乃手書密札曰『持此札者進一階』，命甲賫送。甲至宮門腹痛如割，倩乙代往。明日甲名不與，而乙登籍。太宗驚愕，沉思良久。

passages.text: King Tai-jong was having a rest in Heung-yang Palace, while outside two eunuchs were talking together over the law that governs the affairs of men, as to whether it is man or God. One said, 'Riches and honour are all in the king's hand.' The other said, 'Nothing of the kind; every atom of wealth and every degree of promotion are all ordered of God. Even the king himself has no part in it and no power.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Who Decides, God or the King?' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: The King, overhearing what was said, wrote a secret despatch, saying, 'Raise the Bearer of this letter one degree in rank.' He sealed it and commanded the first eunuch to take it. He made his bow and departed, but just when he was about to leave the palace enclosure a furious pain took him in the stomach, so that he begged his fellow to take his place and go into the city.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Who Decides, God or the King?' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: The next day, when the record of promotions was placed before the King, he read how the second had been advanced, but not one word was there about the first. King Tai-jong made inquiry, and when he knew the circumstances he gave a sudden start of wonder and remained long in deep thought.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Who Decides, God or the King?' (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: Im Sung-jong's Three Years on the Door-sill

region.en: Outside the South Gate, Seoul (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 漢城南門外（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Tale by Yi Ryuk; story of the reign of King Se-jong; English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'Three Things Mastered', eBook #51002

summary.en: Im Sung-jong, a relative of the king and the first performer of his time on the harp, is seen every morning for three years kneeling on the sill of his front door beating his hands up and down on his knees — people think him mad, but thus he learns the motions required for the harp. Night and day he blows and practises with his fingers for three years to learn the motions for the flute; and being light of body and poor at riding and archery, he sighs that he must yet know how to make the bull's-eye, takes his bow into the hills every morning and shoots all day long for three years till he becomes a renowned archer.
summary.zh: 任世宗為王之懿親，善琴。日日跪於門限上以手擊膝，如是者三年，人皆以為狂，而琴法遂成。又畫夜吹簫習指，三年而簫法成。體弱不善騎射，乃日日擕弓矢入山射之，三年而為名射。精誠所至，金石為開。

passages.text: There was a relative of the king, named Im Sung-jong, who was a gifted man in thought and purpose. He was the first performer of his time on the harp. King Se-jong said of him, 'Im's harp knows but one master, and follows no other man.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Three Things Mastered' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: His home was outside the South Gate, and every morning he was seen kneeling on the sill of his front door beating his hands upwards and downwards on his knees, and this practice he carried on for three years. People could not imagine what he meant by it, but thought him mad. Thus he learned the motions required for the harp. Also he blew with his mouth and practised with his fingers day and night without stopping, and kept this up for three years and so learned the motions for the flute.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Three Things Mastered' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: He was a lightly built man in body, and poor at riding and at archery. He often sighed over this defect, and said, 'Though I am weak and stupid and not able to shoot a long distance, I shall yet know how to hit the target and make the bull's-eye. This also must be acquired by practice.' So every morning he took his bow and arrows and went off into the hills, and there he shot all day long, keeping it up for three years, till he became a renowned archer.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Three Things Mastered' (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: The Dead General Who Came Back to Shoot a Thief

texts.period: Tale by Yi Ryuk; story of Kim Tok-saing, honored at the court of Tae-jong; English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'Strangely Stricken Dead', eBook #51002

summary.en: Kim Tok-saing, a soldier of fortune several times generalissimo, has been dead ten years and more when one night his intimate friend is twice awakened with a fright. He has just seen General Kim riding a white horse with bow and arrows at his belt: 'A thief has just entered my home, and I have come to shoot him dead' — and returning, drew an arrow with blood marks on it: 'I have just shot him, he is dead.' In the morning the friend goes to Kim's former home and learns that that very night Kim's young widow had decided to remarry, and as soon as the chosen fiancé entered her home a terrible pain shot him through; before morning he died in great agony.
summary.zh: 金德星歿已十年。一夕其故友連驚醒，言夢見將軍乘白馬佩弓矢來曰『有賊入吾家，吾射殺之矣』，且出矢示之，矢上血痕宛然。晨往其故宅問之，則是夜其寡婦方議改適，所聘者甫入門，暴痛而絕於床。鬼射之說，駭人聽聞。

sensitivity.note: Ancestor-ghost vigilante tale; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: There was once a man called Kim Tok-saing, a soldier of fortune who had been specially honoured at the Court of Tai-jong, and had several times been generalissimo of the army. Kim had been dead now for some ten years and more, when one night this friend of his was awakened with a start and gave a great outcry.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Strangely Stricken Dead' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'I have just seen General Kim riding on a white horse, with bow and arrows at his belt. He called to me and said, A thief has just entered my home, and I have come to shoot him dead. He went and again returned, and as he drew an arrow from his quiver, I saw that there were blood marks on it. He said, I have just shot him, he is dead.' The husband and wife in fear and wonder talked over it together.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Strangely Stricken Dead' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: When morning came the friend went to General Kim's former home to make inquiry. He learned that that very night Kim's young widow had decided to remarry, but as soon as the chosen fiancé had entered her home, a terrible pain shot him through, and before morning came he died in great agony.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Strangely Stricken Dead' (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: The Archers under the Hoi Tree

region.en: Inside the Great East Gate, Seoul (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 漢城東大門內（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Tale by Yi Ryuk; English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'The Mysterious Hoi Tree', eBook #51002

summary.en: Before Prince Pa-song's house inside the great East Gate stands a large Hoi tree. One night the Prince's son-in-law, passing the archers' pavilion, sees a great company of bowmen shooting at the target, practising riding, throwing spears and hurling bowls till the road is blocked. 'Look at that impudent rascal! He attempts to ride by without dismounting.' They catch and beat him till a tall fellow comes out of the ranks: 'He is my master; why do you treat him so?' — undoes his bonds and leads him home. At the gate the son-in-law looks back and sees the man walk under the Hoi tree and disappear: all the crowd of archers were spirits, and the tall one had come forth from their particular Hoi tree.
summary.zh: 怕松公宅在東大門內，門前有海樹一本。其婿夜過射亭，見無數射手習射馳馬擲矛，喧然塞路。眾怒其不下馬，執而笞之。忽有一偉者出曰『此吾主也，何得如此』，為解其縛而送之歸。至門回顧，其人已行入海樹下而滅。蓋群射者皆鬼，偉者即樹中之神也。

passages.text: Prince Pa-song's house was situated just inside of the great East Gate, and before it was a large Hoi tree. On a certain night the Prince's son-in-law was passing by the roadway that led in front of the archers' pavilion. There he saw a great company of bowmen, more than he could number, all shooting together at the target; a moment later he saw them practising riding, some throwing spears, some hurling bowls, some shooting from horseback, so that the road in front of the pavilion was blocked against all comers.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Mysterious Hoi Tree' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: Some shouted as he came by, 'Look at that impudent rascal! He attempts to ride by without dismounting.' They caught him and beat him, paying no attention to his cries for mercy, till one tall fellow came out of their serried ranks and said in an angry voice, 'He is my master; why do you treat him so?' He undid his bonds, took him by the arm and led him home.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Mysterious Hoi Tree' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the son-in-law reached the gate he looked back and saw the man walk under the Hoi tree and disappear. He then learned, too, that all the crowd of archers were spirits and not men, and that the tall one who had befriended him was a spirit too, and that he had come forth from their particular Hoi tree.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'The Mysterious Hoi Tree' (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: Ta-hong, Who Hid Herself until the Honours Came

region.en: Chang-eui ward, Seoul; Keumsan county (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 漢京彰義坊（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Story of Minister Sim Heui-su (1535-1622), told before his death; collected by Im Bang; English ed. Gale, Korean Folk Tales (1913)

source.work: James S. Gale (trans.), Korean Folk Tales (1913), tale 'Ta-hong', eBook #51002

summary.en: At sixteen, the beautiful boy Sim Heui-su sees the kisaeng Ta-hong, Flower-bud, at a banquet and cannot forget her. Days later she alights before him in the street, reveals she asked his name that night, and plights her troth: he must first win first place at the examination and his three days of public rejoicing, and until then she will hide herself in safety. He studies day and night for her sake, marries at his parents' word without joy, and five years after their farewell wins his honours — and on the third evening, called in to an old Minister's house by the Sillai whistle, finds her. For a year she has been a voluntary slave in that house, 'called my concubine in name lest my nephews should steal her away,' confident to the end. She becomes his only wife, forbids their too-frequent happiness as interfereing with duty, and in Keumsan county announces her own death four or five days beforehand: 'Our life is ordered, God decides it all; bury me by my master, that we may meet again.' After her death she still comes to warn him of things to come, never with a mistake, until the dream in which she says 'Master, the time of your departure has come' — and Sim dies the day following, as was foretold.
summary.zh: 沈羲壽十六歲遇名妓桃花（花苞），一見傾心。數日後桃花馬上相認，與之盟曰：『君登科之日乃我歸期，我自匿身以全其節。』沈乃發憤苦讀五年而魁天下。第三日夜誤入某老相公家，桃花果在。原來伊自願為婢於其家，託名側室以避匪人。後為沈正室，賢而克勤。任金山縣令時，桃花預言己死期，至日果卒。遺言葬於夫塋之側。死後猶託夢預告家事，末乃告夫死期，翌日果卒。

sensitivity.note: Love-and-fidelity tale with prophecy; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: Minister Sim Heui-su was, when young, handsome as polished marble and white as the snow. At about sixteen years of age he went with a half-dozen comrades to see a banquet with dancing-girls, where among them was a young woman whose face was very beautiful, not like an earthly person, but like some angelic being: her name was Ta-hong, Flower-bud.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Ta-hong' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: Ten days later, carrying his books along the main street, he suddenly met a pretty girl beautifully dressed, riding a handsome horse, who alighted just in front of him and taking his hand said, 'Are you not Sim Heui-su?' It was Ta-hong. 'I saw you at the gathering, and to me your face was like a god's. From that day on I longed to meet you. Our meeting thus is surely of God's appointment.' They plighted their troth in her aunt's house. 'You have your parents to think of. As I reflect upon your ability and chances for promotion, I see you already a Minister of State. Let us separate just now, and I'll keep myself for you till the time when you win the first place at the Examination and have your three days of public rejoicing. I have a plan by which to hide myself away in safety.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Ta-hong' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: From that time forth, with all his might, he went at his lessons, day and night, not for the sake of the Examination, but for the sake of once more meeting her. It was five years after his farewell to Ta-hong that he won his honours, but on the first day and the second he did not meet her, and the third day was passing with no word. Evening was falling, when his father sent him to call on an old friend in Chang-eui ward; as he was returning, just as he was passing a high gateway, he heard the Sillai call and was obliged to dismount and enter the house of an old Minister, who entertained him and then lifted his glass and inquired, 'Would you like to meet a very beautiful person?' When she came, it was his lost Ta-hong: 'Is this not within the three days of your public celebration, and according to the agreement by which we parted?'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Ta-hong' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: The old man told her history: 'On a certain day this young girl came to us saying, May I have the place of slave with you? I am not running away from any master. She called herself my concubine so as to be safe, lest my nephews or some younger members of the clan should steal her away. We watched the Examination reports, and this time on looking over the list I found your name. She is first of all a faithful woman: I have not known her like before.' His parents gave consent that he should have her, and she was made a member of his family, really his only wife. A little later, as magistrate of Keumsan county, he heard her say one day, 'I am going to die, for my span of life is finished.' In four or five days she fell ill, and a day or two later died, saying, 'Our life is ordered, God decides it all. As I die I ask only that my body be buried where it may rest by the side of my master when he passes away, so that when we meet in the regions beyond I shall be with you once again.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Ta-hong' (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: After her death, whenever anything serious was to happen in his home, she always came to tell him beforehand, and never was there a mistake in her announcements. For several years it has continued thus, till a few days ago she appeared in a dream saying, 'Master, the time of your departure has come, and we are to meet again. I am now making ready for your glad reception.' Last night she came once more and said, 'To-morrow is your day.' In the morning, when he awoke, marks of tears were still upon his cheeks: 'This is not because I fear to die, but because I have seen my Ta-hong.' So Sim died, as was foretold, on the day following.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gale, Korean Folk Tales, 'Ta-hong' (1913); not verbatim.
